The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "How Many High School Stars Make It to the NBA?": https://pudding.cool/2019/03/hype/
The files: data/players.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

# How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan
out?
By
Russell Samora
& Amber Thomas
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in
2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career
in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the
#1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the
NBA, let alone becoming a star?
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve
entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with
some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion
Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes
from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball
careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to
the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 100 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 1,563 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year
rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just
31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA
more often, right?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 10 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 158 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them
eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could
draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a rule was put into place , declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed
from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about reversing this rule , especially in light of the “shoe incident” . Let’s look at the
success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Straight-to-NBA HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 35 players) from 1998 - 2005
Replay
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place.
Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only 15 minutes across 3
games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight
out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better
NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a
US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually
drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our
highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Drafted Top & Unranked HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 779 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of
players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and
ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more
than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook,
Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst
the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are
known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is
college their last stop?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Players from Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and
UNC
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 157 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA
student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how
many yield NBA talent.
# Methods
High school ranking data is based on the Recruiting Services Consensus Index (RSCI) rankings. Data from Basketball Reference . We used a combination
of VORP and Estimated Wins Added to determine the level of success in an NBA career, limiting to the mean
ranking of each player’s top five season. “Superstar” = top 30, “Great” = top 60, “Mediocre” = top 120,
“Below Average” = 120+. H/T to Austin for the idea.

# How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan
out?
By
Russell Samora
& Amber Thomas
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in
2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career
in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the
#1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the
NBA, let alone becoming a star?
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve
entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with
some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion
Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes
from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball
careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to
the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 100 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 1,563 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year
rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just
31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA
more often, right?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 10 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 158 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them
eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could
draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a rule was put into place , declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed
from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about reversing this rule , especially in light of the “shoe incident” . Let’s look at the
success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Straight-to-NBA HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 35 players) from 1998 - 2005
Replay
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place.
Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only 15 minutes across 3
games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight
out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better
NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a
US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually
drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our
highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Drafted Top & Unranked HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 779 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of
players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and
ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more
than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook,
Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst
the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are
known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is
college their last stop?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Players from Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and
UNC
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 157 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA
student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how
many yield NBA talent.
# Methods
High school ranking data is based on the Recruiting Services Consensus Index (RSCI) rankings. Data from Basketball Reference . We used a combination
of VORP and Estimated Wins Added to determine the level of success in an NBA career, limiting to the mean
ranking of each player’s top five season. “Superstar” = top 30, “Great” = top 60, “Mediocre” = top 120,
“Below Average” = 120+. H/T to Austin for the idea.

content.text:
Title: How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2019/03/hype/
Markdown Content:
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan out?
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in 2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the #1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, **are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the NBA, let alone becoming a star?**
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just 31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA more often, right?
High school rank:
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a [rule](https://web.archive.org/web/20080227065646/http://www.nbpa.com/cba_articles/article-X.php) was [put into place](https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/28/sports/basketball/nba-draft-will-close-book-on-high-school-stars.html), declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about [reversing this rule](http://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/26049542/nba-proposes-changing-draft-age-19-18-players-union), especially in light of the [“shoe incident”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqJUgQAyDMo). Let’s look at the success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place. Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only [15 minutes](http://www.basketball-reference.com/players/y/youngko01.html) across 3 games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook, Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is college their last stop?
High school rank:
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how many yield NBA talent.

Title: How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2019/03/hype/index.html
Markdown Content:
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan out?
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in 2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the #1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, **are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the NBA, let alone becoming a star?**
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just 31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA more often, right?
High school rank:
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a [rule](https://web.archive.org/web/20080227065646/http://www.nbpa.com/cba_articles/article-X.php) was [put into place](https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/28/sports/basketball/nba-draft-will-close-book-on-high-school-stars.html), declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about [reversing this rule](http://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/26049542/nba-proposes-changing-draft-age-19-18-players-union), especially in light of the [“shoe incident”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqJUgQAyDMo). Let’s look at the success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place. Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only [15 minutes](http://www.basketball-reference.com/players/y/youngko01.html) across 3 games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook, Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is college their last stop?
High school rank:
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how many yield NBA talent.

content.text:
Title: How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2019/03/hype/?x-respond-with=html
Markdown Content:
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan out?
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in 2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the #1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, **are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the NBA, let alone becoming a star?**
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just 31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA more often, right?
High school rank:
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a [rule](https://web.archive.org/web/20080227065646/http://www.nbpa.com/cba_articles/article-X.php) was [put into place](https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/28/sports/basketball/nba-draft-will-close-book-on-high-school-stars.html), declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about [reversing this rule](http://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/26049542/nba-proposes-changing-draft-age-19-18-players-union), especially in light of the [“shoe incident”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LqJUgQAyDMo). Let’s look at the success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place. Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only [15 minutes](http://www.basketball-reference.com/players/y/youngko01.html) across 3 games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook, Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is college their last stop?
High school rank:
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how many yield NBA talent.

# How many high school stars make it in the NBA?
Every year the top high school basketball recruits get hyped up. How often do they pan
out?
By
Russell Samora
& Amber Thomas
🏀
Feb 2019
Remember NBA great Donnell Harvey? Neither do we. Despite being the #1 high school recruit in
2000—something that you think would indicate future NBA stardom—he put together a meager career
in the league, averaging around 5 points per game over 5 years. On the flip side is LeBron James—the
#1 high school recruit just a few years later—and we all know what he’s been up to.
This disparity got us thinking, are these top 100 recruit lists any indication of making it to the
NBA, let alone becoming a star?
It must be really hard to assess top talent when the pool is so large in high school. Now that we’ve
entered the YouTube era, hype surrounding players can inflate in an instant. Sure, LeBron paved the way with
some nationally televised games, but now millions of people are watching Zion
Williamson throw down dunks in warm ups, or Lamelo Ball hit threes
from half court in eight grade.
Let’s take a look at just how far the high school stars of the past 20 years made it in their basketball
careers.
Below, each circle is a player that ranked amongst the top 100 high school recruits in the US according to
the Recruiting Services Consensus Index.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 100 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 1,563 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
27% of the 1,563 top-ranked high school players made it to the NBA and only 25% made it past their two-year
rookie contract. Put another way, 441 of the 900 draft picks in that 15 year span were top 100 recruits. Just
31 players eventually reached “superstar” status (based on advanced statistics, details at the bottom).
But perhaps the top 100 is too broad of a categorization. Surely the top 10 players will make it to the NBA
more often, right?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Top 10 High School Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 158 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Players ranked in the top 10 certainly appear to have slightly better odds—a full 84% of them
eventually made it to the NBA. Though with 60 draft picks a year, you might expect that number to be higher.
In the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, teams could bet hard enough on a player’s future success that they could
draft them straight out of high school. This ended in 2006 when a rule was put into place , declaring that players had to be at least 19 years old or one year removed
from high school before getting drafted. But talks are escalating about reversing this rule , especially in light of the “shoe incident” . Let’s look at the
success of the straight-to-NBA high school players.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Straight-to-NBA HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 35 players) from 1998 - 2005
Replay
Opponents of removing the age limit often cite players like Korleone Young as reasons to keep it in place.
Young, the #3 ranked high school player in 1998, ultimately fizzled out of the NBA having played only 15 minutes across 3
games. However, he appears to be the exception more than the rule. Of the other 34 players drafted straight
out of high school, 94% made it past their rookie contract, with 55% eventually becoming mediocre or better
NBA players.
Let’s switch our view once more, away from the highest ranking high school players to those that played in a
US high school, but did not appear on the top 100 list. We found 338 of these players that were eventually
drafted into the NBA, despite being undervalued in high school. Let’s compare their career paths with our
highly-ranked and drafted high schoolers.
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Drafted Top & Unranked HS Players
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 779 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
Even when we limit the top ranked players to just those that were eventually drafted, the success rate of
players ranked in high school is notably higher than for those who weren’t. Where 92% of the drafted and
ranked players made it past their rookie contract, only 73% of the unranked and drafted players stayed more
than two years. Seven players—Dwyane Wade, Marc Gasol, Paul George, Jimmy Butler,Russell Westbrook,
Stephen Curry, and Damian Lillard—whose high school careers were apparently not worthy of a spot amongst
the top 100, still broke into the ranks of superstars in their NBA careers.
Let’s look at one more slice that has lofty expectations; The Big 4. Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and UNC are
known to consistently land the biggest recruits. Do these recruits translate into NBA success stories or is
college their last stop?
High school rank:
# Level Reached of Players from Kentucky, Kansas, Duke, and
UNC
Percentage of players that reach each level (out of 157 players) from 1998 - 2013
Replay
The college funnel is an interesting discussion, especially when it surrounds the lack of pay for NCAA
student athletes. Below we widen the field to take a look at the biggest NBA-producing colleges and see how
many yield NBA talent.
# Methods
High school ranking data is based on the Recruiting Services Consensus Index (RSCI) rankings. Data from Basketball Reference . We used a combination
of VORP and Estimated Wins Added to determine the level of success in an NBA career, limiting to the mean
ranking of each player’s top five season. “Superstar” = top 30, “Great” = top 60, “Mediocre” = top 120,
“Below Average” = 120+. H/T to Austin for the idea.
